findings.issue_text: In parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts, computed schema keys using z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() both evaluate to the same string, causing the second key to overwrite the first, so minimumTokenResponseSchema doesn't implement the intended match-any/allow-arbitrary behavior and ends up with only access_token and one meaningless key.

In googlecalendar CalendarService.ts, parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a ZodSafeParseResult wrapper but the code assigns it directly to key in prisma.credential.update, storing the safe-parse wrapper instead of the actual parsed credential object.

In googlecalendar CalendarService.ts, when credential sharing is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but the code accesses res?.data expecting the Google API library's axios-shaped response, so token will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime.

In hubspot CalendarService.ts, when credential sharing is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but the return value is assigned to hubspotRefreshToken and subsequent code accesses .access_token and .refresh_token directly, which a Response doesn't have, so token extraction will fail.

In zoho-bigin CalendarService.ts, when credential sharing is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but the code accesses tokenInfo.data.error expecting an axios response shape; a Response has no .data property, so tokenInfo.data is undefined and the check will throw.

In zohocrm CalendarService.ts, same axios-vs-fetch mismatch: when sharing is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response but the code accesses zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error expecting an axios response shape.

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: In parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts, computed schema keys using z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() both evaluate to the same string, causing the second key to overwrite the first, so minimumTokenResponseSchema doesn't implement the intended match-any/allow-arbitrary behavior and ends up with only access_token and one meaningless key.

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is declared with computed property keys: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. Those computed keys are evaluated immediately to plain JS string keys at object-literal creation time, and they will not represent “any string key”; they will be whatever `toString()` returns for those Zod schema objects. Since both expressions are effectively constant strings (and very likely the same string), the latter property will overwrite the former in the object literal. As a result, the schema does not implement the intended ‘match any numeric expiry fields + allow arbitrary fields’ behavior (Zod requires `z.record(...)` or `.catchall(...)` for that).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing try/catch around `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` in `app-credential.ts`, causing unhandled exceptions for tampered or invalid ciphertext
Webhook secret compared with `!==` in `app-credential.ts` is timing-unsafe, should use constant-time comparison like `crypto.timingSafeEqual`

adjudication.rationale:
In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook secret is validated via a direct string inequality check:

```ts
req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET
```

A normal `===`/`!==` string comparison is not guaranteed to be constant-time and may short-circuit on the first mismatched character, which can leak information via timing differences. For secret validation (webhook/shared-secret auth), a constant-time comparison (e.g., `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on `Buffer`s) is the safer approach. This is a real security weakness introduced/visible in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Empty webhook secret in `app-credential.ts` allows authorization bypass due to missing guard rejecting empty/unset secrets

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, auth is only `req.headers[headerName] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. There is no guard that `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is set/non-empty. If the env var is unset (`undefined`) and the request omits the header (also `undefined`), the comparison is false and the request is authorized. Even if the env var is set to an empty string, a client can send an empty header value to match it. This creates an authorization bypass when the secret is misconfigured/empty.

adjudication_records.issue_text: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses [z.string().toString()] as computed object keys, causing both dynamic keys to collapse to '[object Object]' instead of implementing the intended 'any numeric property = expiry' and 'allow other properties' logic

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is defined as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. Both computed keys evaluate immediately at definition time, and `z.string()`/`z.string().optional()` are objects whose `.toString()` results in the same string key (effectively `"[object Object]"`). That means the two computed properties collide and one overwrites the other, and it does not implement an index-signature-like "any numeric property" / "allow other properties" behavior. Zod object schemas also don't work that way for arbitrary keys; this is a functional defect in the schema as written.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refreshOAuthTokens returns fundamentally different types in its two branches (Response from fetch vs parsed object from refreshFunction), causing runtime failures when callers access properties like .data.error on the enabled path

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, the enabled branch does `return response;` where `response` is the result of `fetch(CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)`, i.e. a standard Fetch `Response`. The else branch returns whatever `refreshFunction()` returns (often a parsed token object or a non-Fetch HTTP response). Callers assume specific shapes: e.g. `GoogleCalendarService` assigns `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...); const token = res?.data;` which works when `refreshFunction` returns a Gaxios-like response with `.data`, but will fail when syncing is enabled because Fetch `Response` has no `.data`. Similarly, `HubspotCalendarService` types the result as `HubspotToken` (an object from the HubSpot SDK), but on the enabled path it would instead receive a Fetch `Response`, breaking subsequent property access. This is a concrete, diff-verifiable runtime incompatibility introduced by the wrapper.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts is structurally broken as computed keys collapse to the same property name and do not capture intended semantics

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `minimumTokenResponseSchema`, the object literal uses computed property names `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. Those expressions evaluate to a *single string key* at runtime (e.g. "[object Object]" or similar), so they do not create a wildcard/dynamic key schema. Additionally, both computed keys likely resolve to the same string, so the latter entry overwrites the former in the object shape. As a result, the schema does not actually mean “any numeric property is expiry” / “allow other properties”; it just defines one (possibly overwritten) fixed property name, making the intended semantics incorrect and the schema effectively broken.

adjudication_records.issue_text: refresh_token is set to the literal string "refresh_token" when missing, breaking OAuth for that user instead of preserving the existing refresh token

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, when the parsed token response lacks `refresh_token`, it explicitly sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. In `Office365CalendarService`, the result is then merged into existing credentials via `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) }`. Because `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on failure, `tokenResponse.success` is effectively always true, so `tokenResponse.data.refresh_token` will overwrite the previously stored real refresh token with the literal string when the refresh response omits it (which is common, especially under the new APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED + CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT path that only requires access token + expiry). That would break future refreshes for that user.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Persists the entire SafeParseReturnType object as the credential key instead of just the parsed data

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the diff changes `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials);` (which returns the parsed data) to `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);`. But `parseRefreshTokenResponse` calls `schema.safeParse(...)` and returns the *SafeParseReturnType* object (`{ success, data, error }`), not `data`. That returned object is then persisted via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, meaning the credential `key` would store the entire safeParse result wrapper rather than just the parsed credential payload.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Inconsistent return types between the sync-endpoint and local branches in refreshOAuthTokens.ts break callers

adjudication.rationale: Yes. `refreshOAuthTokens` returns different shapes depending on the branch: when syncing is enabled it returns the raw `fetch()` `Response`, but in the non-sync branch it returns whatever `refreshFunction()` returns (often a parsed token object or a non-Fetch response). Callers assume a specific type. For example, `HubspotCalendarService` types the result as `HubspotToken`, but under the sync branch it would receive a `Response` instead. Similarly, `GoogleCalendarService` expects `res.data` (from `myGoogleAuth.refreshToken(...).res`), but under the sync branch `res` is a Fetch `Response` with no `.data`, so `token.access_token` will be undefined and subsequent logic breaks. This inconsistency is directly verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Sync endpoint call has no authentication, error handling, or response validation, allowing anyone to request fresh access tokens

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, the server makes a POST to the sync endpoint with only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body and no authentication material (no secret header, token, signature, etc.). It also does no error handling (`response.ok` is never checked) and returns the raw `fetch` response without parsing/validating it. Call sites then assume a successful, correctly-shaped token response (e.g., Google reads `res?.data`), so an untrusted/unprotected endpoint could be queried without proof-of-origin and failures/bad responses are not handled/validated here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Encryption key silently falls back to an empty string if the environment variable is unset instead of failing fast

adjudication.rationale: In the new webhook handler (`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`), decryption uses `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")`. If `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is unset, it will pass an empty string as the key rather than rejecting the request or throwing immediately based on missing configuration. There is no prior validation/check that the env var is present, so this is a verifiable “silent fallback” instead of failing fast.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook secret is compared using non-constant-time string inequality, creating a timing oracle

adjudication.rationale:
In the new API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook secret is validated with a direct string inequality check:

```ts
if (req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET)
```

This uses normal JS string comparison, which is not guaranteed to be constant-time and can short-circuit based on early mismatches/length, so it can theoretically leak information via timing differences when an attacker can probe the endpoint repeatedly. A timing-safe compare (e.g., `crypto.timingSafeEqual` after normalizing to buffers) would avoid that class of oracle.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Caller-provided schema is discarded when sync is enabled, falling back to a broken minimumTokenResponseSchema that fails to enforce app-specific invariants

adjudication.rationale:
Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is true, the function ignores the caller-provided `schema` and instead uses `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)`, so any app-specific validation/invariants in `schema` are not applied.

Additionally, the `minimumTokenResponseSchema` itself is effectively broken: it tries to express “any numeric property” via computed keys `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: ...`, but in a JS object literal these become a single literal property name (e.g., `"[object Object]"`/similar), not a pattern for arbitrary keys. That means typical OAuth token responses (with `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, etc.) will not match and `safeParse` will likely fail. Even if it did parse, the code then weakens invariants further by forcibly setting a dummy `refresh_token` (`"refresh_token"`) when missing.

So the finding about discarding the caller schema and falling back to a non-enforcing (and likely non-working) minimum schema is directly supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Header name lookup is case-sensitive against a user-controlled environment variable, causing silent mismatches

adjudication.rationale:
In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the secret check indexes `req.headers[...]` using `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` directly:

```ts
req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]
```

In Node/Next.js, `req.headers` keys are normalized to lowercase. If the env var is set to a non-lowercase value (e.g., `Calcom-Webhook-Secret`), this lookup will return `undefined` and the request will be rejected with 403 even if the header is present. The `.env.example` even warns it “should be in lowercase”, but the code does not enforce/normalize it, so a case mismatch is a real, verifiable correctness defect introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: userId: null is silently treated as "use local refresh", conflating distinct conditions and misrouting falsy but valid IDs

adjudication.rationale: In `refreshOAuthTokens`, the decision to use the sync endpoint is gated by `&& userId` (truthiness) even though `userId` is typed as `number | null`. This means `null` and any falsy numeric ID (e.g., `0`) are treated the same and will fall back to the local refresh path. That conflates “no user” with “user ID is 0”, and could misroute requests if `0` is ever a valid userId. A stricter check like `userId !== null` would avoid this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys collapse to '[object Object]', breaking wildcard-key matching and schema validation

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is defined as a `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. Those computed property names are evaluated immediately as plain strings (e.g., `z.string()` is an object and `toString()` will yield a constant like "[object Object]" or similar), so they do not create wildcard/"any key" matching. The schema will only accept literal keys with those exact names, breaking the intended validation of arbitrary numeric expiry fields and arbitrary extra fields. Zod requires `z.record(...)` or `.catchall(...)` for this behavior.

Previously the code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returns the credential object shape. This change will store a different/wrong shape in `credential.key`, breaking expected credential structure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse uses 'any' parameter type, undermining TypeScript safety and schema validation

adjudication.rationale: In the added `parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the function signature is `const parseRefreshTokenResponse = (response: any, schema: z.ZodTypeAny) => { ... }`. While `any` does reduce compile-time TypeScript checking, the function immediately applies Zod runtime validation via `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)` or `schema.safeParse(response)`. That means schema validation is not “undermined” by the `any` type here; it’s still enforced at runtime. adjudication_records.issue_text: Timing-unsafe comparison (`!==`) of the webhook shared secret instead of using `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, allowing timing attacks to recover the secret.

adjudication.rationale:
In the new API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook secret is validated via a direct inequality check:

```ts
if (req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET)
```

This is a normal string/primitive comparison and is not designed to be constant-time. Comparing a shared secret this way can leak information via timing differences (early-exit comparisons), so the finding correctly identifies a real security weakness introduced in the diff (a timing-safe comparison like `crypto.timingSafeEqual` is the typical mitigation).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Broken Zod 'minimum' schema uses computed object-literal keys that resolve to the same literal, causing it to only validate `access_token` and skip validation of other fields, allowing malformed data to be persisted.

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is defined as a `z.object({ access_token: ..., [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: ... })`. Those computed property keys are evaluated immediately to plain strings (and very likely to the same string), so they do not express “any string key” constraints. In practice this leaves the schema only reliably validating `access_token` while treating other response fields (like `expiry_date`/`expires_in`) as unknown keys that Zod will not validate (and will strip by default), defeating the intended minimum validation and allowing malformed token responses through when the minimum schema path is used.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `refresh_token` is defaulted to the literal string `'refresh_token'` when missing, corrupting the credential and permanently breaking integrations on the next refresh cycle.
matched_golden_ids: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook authorizes cross-tenant credential writes using a single global secret without per-user or per-org scoping, allowing credential overwrites for any user (IDOR).

adjudication.rationale: The new endpoint `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` authorizes requests solely by comparing a single global shared secret header (`req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`) to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. After that, it accepts an arbitrary `userId` from the body and performs `prisma.credential.update/create` for that `userId` + `appSlug` without any per-tenant/per-org/per-user scoping or additional authorization checks. This means anyone who can send requests with the global secret can overwrite/create credentials for *any* user ID on the instance (classic IDOR-style “object reference by userId” under a shared-secret auth model).

adjudication_records.issue_text: `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` response is consumed without validating the status code (`response.ok`) or validating the endpoint's scheme/host, creating an SSRF risk.
